title: What Running 26.2 Miles Does to Your Body, Mile by Mile
description:
A marathon pushes your fuel tanks, your fluid balance, your kidneys and your heart further than almost anything else people do for fun. Follow a runner from the start line to the finish and see what the science says is happening inside, including why the wall hits around mile twenty.

Sources:
- Nutrition Reviews (2018), Fundamentals of glycogen metabolism for coaches and athletes: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6019055/
- Frontiers in Medicine (2017), Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia: 2017 Update: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5334560
- Yale News (2017), Marathon running may cause short-term kidney injury: https://news.yale.edu/2017/03/28/marathon-running-may-cause-short-term-kidney-injury
- The Hospitalist, Marathon runners are at low risk of cardiac arrest (RACER study, NEJM 2012): https://blogs.the-hospitalist.org/content/marathon-runners-are-low-risk-cardiac-arrest

This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice.

scenes.narration: Twenty six point two miles. Somewhere around mile twenty, many runners feel like they have hit a wall. Here is what is happening inside them.
scenes.headline: WHY RUNNERS HIT THE WALL

visual.query: tired marathon runner late in race
visual.note: a determined runner pushing through fatigue late in a race

scenes.narration: Every year, huge numbers of people take on this distance. In the United States alone, more than half a million people ran a marathon in two thousand fifteen. Most are not elite athletes. They are teachers, nurses and accountants who spent months training for one long morning.
scenes.headline: HALF A MILLION RUNNERS
scenes.sub: In one year, in the US

visual.note: a crowd of marathon runners filling a city street

scenes.narration: A marathon is a fascinating experiment because it pushes several of your body's systems toward their limits at once: your fuel supply, your water balance, your kidneys and your heart. So follow one runner, mile by mile, and watch each system respond.
scenes.headline: ONE RACE, FOUR SYSTEMS

visual.spec: a marathon course line from start to finish with four icons along it: fuel tank, water drop, kidney, heart

scenes.narration: The starting gun fires. Within seconds, your heart speeds up and your breathing deepens, sending more oxygen to your leg muscles. Those muscles need fuel to keep contracting, step after step, and they have two main tanks to draw from: carbohydrate and fat.
scenes.headline: MILE ZERO: TWO FUEL TANKS

visual.note: runners surging forward at a marathon start line

scenes.narration: Your carbohydrate tank is called glycogen, chains of glucose packed into your muscles and liver. Your whole body holds roughly six hundred grams of it. About five hundred grams sit in your muscles, and about eighty grams in your liver, which uses its supply to keep your blood sugar steady.
scenes.headline: THE GLYCOGEN TANK

visual.spec: human outline with glycogen stores highlighted: large amount in leg and arm muscles, smaller amount in the liver, with gram labels

scenes.narration: Your fat tank is far bigger, even in very lean runners. But fat has a drawback. Your body breaks it down more slowly. At the faster, harder paces of a race, your muscles lean more heavily on glucose and glycogen, because carbohydrate can be turned into energy quickly.
scenes.headline: FAT IS BIG BUT SLOW

visual.note: microscope image of fat cells

scenes.narration: Push the distance far enough, and that balance flips. In ultra-endurance events, which can last many hours or even days, the pace drops low enough that burning fat normally predominates. A marathon sits in a tricky middle zone: long enough to drain glycogen, fast enough to depend on it.
scenes.headline: THE MARATHON MIDDLE ZONE

visual.spec: a horizontal scale from sprint to marathon to ultramarathon, showing fuel use shifting from mostly carbohydrate to mostly fat

scenes.narration: Here is a surprising fact about that glycogen. Every gram of it is stored with at least three grams of water. So your fuel tank is also a water tank. As you burn through glycogen, that water is released.
scenes.headline: YOUR FUEL IS WET
scenes.sub: Three grams of water per gram

visual.spec: one glycogen granule surrounded by three water droplets, labeled 1 gram glycogen and at least 3 grams water

scenes.narration: By mile ten, things feel good. Your muscles are warm, your stride is smooth, and your body is burning a mix of carbohydrate and fat. But that steady pace is quietly draining your muscle glycogen, and remember, the tank has a bottom.
scenes.headline: MILE TEN: CRUISING

visual.note: runners looking relaxed and steady mid-race

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, you are heating up. Working muscles generate heat, and to dump it, your body sweats. Sweat cools you as it evaporates, but it costs water and some salt. So most runners grab cups at aid stations along the way.
scenes.headline: THE HEAT BUILDS

visual.note: volunteers handing out cups at a race water station

scenes.narration: Now here is something many people get backward. You might think the main fluid danger in a marathon is not drinking enough. But researchers have found that one well-documented risk comes from drinking too much.
scenes.headline: THE OPPOSITE DANGER

visual.note: a runner drinking from a bottle

scenes.narration: It is called exercise-associated hyponatremia, which means the sodium in your blood becomes too diluted. Sodium is a key salt your cells depend on. When blood sodium falls too low, it can become a serious medical emergency.
scenes.headline: WHEN BLOOD GETS DILUTED

visual.spec: two beakers of blood: left with normal sodium particles, right with the same particles spread through much more water, labeled diluted

scenes.narration: A major review describes the main cause as drinking beyond thirst, combined with a hormone called vasopressin. Normally, vasopressin tells your kidneys to hold on to water. During the stress of long exercise, it can stay switched on, so extra water gets retained instead of passed.
scenes.headline: DRINKING BEYOND THIRST

visual.note: the pituitary gland at the base of the brain, which releases vasopressin

scenes.narration: Exercise is not the only thing that keeps vasopressin switched on. Heat, nausea and low blood sugar can push it up too, and those tend to pile up late in a long, hot race. And this is not just a runner's problem. Screening studies have found low sodium in triathletes, cyclists, rowers and even rugby players.
scenes.headline: NOT JUST RUNNERS
scenes.sub: Heat, nausea and low blood sugar

visual.note: cyclists racing during a triathlon

scenes.narration: Screening studies have found low blood sodium without symptoms in anywhere from about five percent to seventy percent of athletes, depending on the event and when they were tested. That is one reason sports medicine experts now emphasize drinking according to thirst rather than forcing down fixed amounts.
scenes.headline: LET THIRST GUIDE

visual.note: a medical tent near a race finish area

scenes.narration: Around mile eighteen, your fuel gauge is dropping fast. And over the next few miles, many runners experience the most famous moment in endurance sport. Their legs turn heavy, their pace collapses, and every step feels like wading through sand.
scenes.headline: MILE EIGHTEEN: RUNNING LOW

visual.note: a runner slowing to a walk, looking exhausted

scenes.narration: Runners call it hitting the wall. Scientists describe the core of it more plainly. The depletion of muscle glycogen causes fatigue. When glycogen runs low, your muscles cannot produce energy fast enough to sustain the same pace.
scenes.headline: HITTING THE WALL

visual.spec: a fuel gauge for muscle glycogen dropping from full at the start line to nearly empty around mile 20

scenes.narration: There is even a mechanism at the cellular level. When glycogen inside a muscle fiber falls very low, the fiber has trouble releasing the calcium it needs to contract, and its power output drops. Your muscle is not refusing to work. It is running short of the means to work hard.
scenes.headline: A CALCIUM SHORTAGE

visual.note: microscope image of striated muscle fibers

scenes.narration: This is also where training shows. Months of endurance training shift your muscles toward burning more fat, which spares precious glycogen for later. That is part of why well-trained runners can hold their pace deeper into the race.
scenes.headline: TRAINING SPARES FUEL

visual.note: a runner training alone on a quiet road at dawn

scenes.narration: Somehow you push through, and you cross the finish line. The race is over, but inside your body, some of the most interesting changes are only now showing up. Two organs in particular have been working overtime: your kidneys and your heart.
scenes.headline: THE FINISH LINE

visual.note: a runner crossing the finish line with arms raised

scenes.narration: In a Yale-led study, researchers took blood and urine samples from runners before and after the Hartford Marathon. Soon after the race, eighty two percent of the runners showed signs of stage one acute kidney injury, the mildest category.
scenes.headline: KIDNEYS UNDER STRESS

visual.note: cross-section illustration of a kidney

scenes.narration: That sounds alarming, but the changes resolved within about two days. Researchers suspect a mix of causes: a sustained rise in body temperature, dehydration, and reduced blood flow to the kidneys. The long-term effects are not yet clear.
scenes.headline: GONE IN ABOUT TWO DAYS

visual.spec: timeline: kidney stress marker rising at the finish line and returning to baseline about two days later

scenes.narration: The study was small, and the lead researcher said it needs to be investigated further. He also noted that research has shown changes in heart function linked to marathon running. Which brings up the question many people quietly wonder about.
scenes.headline: WHAT ABOUT THE HEART?

visual.query: runner checking heart rate monitor watch
visual.note: a runner glancing at a heart rate watch

scenes.narration: Is running a marathon dangerous for your heart? Researchers studied about ten point nine million participants in American marathons and half marathons over a decade. They found about one cardiac arrest for every one hundred eighty four thousand participants.
scenes.headline: ONE IN 184,000

visual.note: an anatomical illustration of the heart

scenes.narration: So the overall risk is low. But it is not zero, and it was higher in full marathons than half marathons, and in men than in women. When a cause could be found, the most common was a thickening of the heart muscle called hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
scenes.headline: LOW, BUT NOT ZERO

visual.note: a doctor reviewing heart test results with a patient

scenes.narration: That is why medical teams line marathon courses, and why anyone thinking about training for one is encouraged to talk with a doctor first. Building up gradually, over months, gives every one of these systems time to adapt.
scenes.headline: TALK TO A DOCTOR FIRST

visual.note: a person talking with a doctor in a clinic

scenes.narration: In the hours after the race, your body starts refilling its tanks. Muscles rebuild their glycogen. And because each gram of glycogen pulls water back in with it, part of the weight you lost during the race returns as that fuel is restored.
scenes.headline: REFILLING THE TANKS

visual.query: runners resting after race with medals
visual.note: runners resting and recovering with finisher medals

scenes.narration: So what does a marathon really do to your body? It drains a fuel tank you carry in your muscles. It tests how well you balance water and salt. It briefly stresses your kidneys. And it asks your heart to work hard for hours.
scenes.headline: WHAT 26.2 MILES REALLY DOES

visual.spec: summary graphic of a runner with four labeled callouts: glycogen drained, water and salt balance, kidneys stressed briefly, heart working for hours

scenes.narration: And yet, after months of preparation, ordinary bodies cover the distance by the hundreds of thousands. Few things show so clearly that your body is not fixed. Give it time and a steady challenge, and it rebuilds itself to meet it.
scenes.headline: BODIES THAT ADAPT

visual.query: diverse group of runners finishing race
visual.note: a diverse group of runners of all ages finishing together

scenes.narration: Follow Inside Your Body for more of the science of you.
